passage:
Deepika ran into the courtyard with her cheeks burning. Her wooden bullock cart lay on the mud, one wheel snapped off. "Bhupen! I told you not to touch it!" she shouted. Her little brother was not there. She found him behind the big water pot, curled up, the wheel in both hands, his whole body shaking.
Then she remembered him going silent for a whole day after Baba scolded him for dropping the milk can. His eyes were wide and wet.
"Did you think I would hit you?" she asked, slowly. Bhupen nodded. Deepika took a breath. She was still angry, and the anger tugged at her again when she looked at the cart. But she sat down beside him. "Give me the wheel. We'll ask Dada to fix it."

qa.q: Where did Deepika find Bhupen?
qa.a: She found him behind the big water pot, holding the wheel in both hands.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she found Bhupen and then looked at the cart again?
qa.a: She was still angry, and the anger tugged at her again. But it was mixed with sympathy once she saw how frightened he was.

qa.q: What small step let Deepika stay calm even though she was still angry?
qa.a: She asked him a quiet question and then offered a plan to fix the cart. Taking a breath and sitting beside him gave the anger time to settle.

qa.q: How did Bhupen see Deepika's first shout?
qa.a: As frightening. He hid behind the water pot, shook and had wide wet eyes, which suggests he thought she might hit him.

grounding: A child realises her brother who broke a toy was frightened, not being unkind, though her anger still tugs at her.

passage:
Thabo's model plane had taken three weeks to build. Now the left wing lay in two pieces on the living-room floor. "You wrecked it!" Thabo yelled. His hands were shaking with rage. "You never listen, Kaito!"
His younger brother stood very still by the sofa, holding a wet sock in one hand. He had gone pale. He didn't argue, and he didn't leave.
Thabo stopped. Kaito never went quiet like that. "Were you trying to put it back on the shelf?" Thabo asked. Kaito nodded, tears sliding down. "I knocked it. I was scared you'd be angry, so I just stood here."
Thabo's anger flared up again when he saw the wing. He breathed out slowly. "Get the glue. It will still fly, sort of."

qa.q: How long had Thabo's model plane taken to build?
qa.a: It had taken three weeks to build.

qa.q: What was Thabo feeling when he saw the wing and then looked at Kaito?
qa.a: He was furious at first and the anger flared again at the sight of the wing. Seeing Kaito go pale and silent added worry and made him stop.

qa.q: What could Thabo do next to keep the repair from turning into another fight?
qa.a: He could work on the glue job together with Kaito and let his own anger cool first. Giving Kaito a job helps him feel forgiven.

qa.q: What is it like for Kaito to be shouted at over an accident?
qa.a: It is scary and lonely. He did not argue or run, which suggests he felt he deserved it, and he needed to hear he was not being blamed for meanness.

grounding: A child sees that his brother who broke the toy was afraid, and holds onto that view though anger returns.

passage:
"My kaleidoscope! Who did this?" Ankita held up the cracked tube, bits of coloured glass on the floor.
Silence. Then a small shuffle under the bed.
"Nazia. Come out right now."
"No."
"You broke it on purpose because I didn't let you play!"
"I didn't!" Nazia's voice wobbled. "I was just looking. It fell. I thought you'd hate me forever."
Ankita crouched. Her little sister's face was red and wet, and her hands were shaking.
"You hid because you were scared?"
A nod.
Ankita breathed out. "I don't hate you. I'm just really, really cross."
"Can we fix it?"
"Maybe with tape." Ankita picked up a blue piece, and her jaw tightened again. "But you're not touching my things for a week."
"Okay," whispered Nazia, crawling out slowly.

qa.q: Where was Nazia hiding?
qa.a: She was under the bed.

qa.q: What did Ankita realise when she saw Nazia's face, and how did she still feel?
qa.a: She realised Nazia had hidden because she was scared, not mean, but she still felt really cross, and the anger came back when she picked up the broken glass.

qa.q: What small step could help the sisters after this?
qa.a: They could fix the kaleidoscope together with tape, so Nazia can make up for it and Ankita can calm down while doing something useful.

qa.q: How did Nazia see what happened?
qa.a: To Nazia it was an accident while looking, and she was so frightened of losing her sister's love that she hid instead of saying sorry.

grounding: Shows a child seeing that a sibling who broke her toy was frightened, not mean, though the anger keeps returning.

passage:
Mum shouted "Amandeep, dinner!" at the exact moment I found my remote car behind the sofa with one wheel snapped off. I knew who did it. Pooja, my little sister, had been driving it into walls all afternoon.
I stomped into the kitchen ready to yell. Pooja was sitting very still, not eating, looking at her plate. When she saw the car in my hand, she started crying before I said anything.
I wanted to be angry. I was angry. But she looked like I look when I break something of Mum's and wait for trouble.
So I just said, "It was an accident, na?" She nodded so fast.
I'd like to say I stayed nice. I didn't. At bedtime the wheel still wouldn't click in, and I told her she ruined everything.

qa.q: What was broken on Amandeep's remote car?
qa.a: One wheel was snapped off.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling on seeing Pooja at the table?
qa.a: Amandeep was angry but also recognised Pooja's fear, because she looked the way Amandeep looks when waiting for trouble, so the anger softened for a while.

qa.q: What could Amandeep try at bedtime when the anger comes back?
qa.a: Amandeep could take a few breaths, put the car down for the night and say 'I'm still upset, let's try fixing it tomorrow' instead of blaming Pooja.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Pooja at dinner?
qa.a: Pooja was probably scared and guilty, sitting still and not eating while she waited to be shouted at.

grounding: Shows a child realising a sibling who broke a toy was scared rather than mean, and how hard that understanding is to hold onto.

passage:
After-school centre, Thursday note.
Jatin (11) came in from the craft room holding his clay temple, one tower crushed. He went straight to Sahil, his younger brother, and grabbed his sleeve. "You sat on it!" Sahil did not argue. He stood rigid, eyes on the floor, then whispered, "Please don't tell Mummy."
Jatin let go. He asked, quite quietly, "Why are you so scared?" Sahil said Mummy had told him to be careful near Jatin's projects. Jatin looked at the crushed tower for a long time and said, "It's okay, it was clay."
Ten minutes later, when another child laughed at the temple, Jatin snapped at Sahil again.
I sat with both boys, helped them reshape the tower together, and mentioned the good moment to their mother at pickup.

qa.q: What did Sahil whisper when Jatin grabbed his sleeve?
qa.a: He whispered, 'Please don't tell Mummy.'

qa.q: What changed in Jatin when he asked Sahil why he was so scared?
qa.a: Jatin's anger eased into understanding; he seemed to feel sorry for Sahil once he saw his brother was frightened, not careless on purpose.

qa.q: What did the note-writer do next, and why did it help?
qa.a: They sat with both boys and helped them reshape the tower together, which let Jatin cool down and let Sahil make amends.

qa.q: How might Sahil see the moment when Jatin said it was only clay?
qa.a: Sahil was probably hugely relieved, since he had been expecting trouble and his brother chose kindness instead.

grounding: Shows a child briefly understanding that his brother broke his model out of fear, not meanness, before anger returns.

passage:
Saturday
Jomon's diary. Devika broke my ship model today. The one with the matchstick mast that took me two weeks. I found it in pieces behind the sofa and shouted so loud that Amma came running. I called Devika a destroyer and said I hate her. She didn't even cry. She just hid under the dining table.
After dinner I was still angry. But then I remembered she was hiding, not laughing. When I break something at Ammachi's house I hide too, because I'm scared, not because I wanted it broken. Maybe she was scared of me.
I told her I'm not angry anymore. That was only half true. The mast is still broken.

qa.q: How long did the ship model take Jomon to make?
qa.a: It took two weeks.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling after dinner?
qa.a: Jomon still felt angry about the ship but also started to feel sorry, realising Devika had hidden because she was scared, not mean.

qa.q: What could Jomon and Devika do together about the broken mast?
qa.a: They could glue the mast together, and Jomon could calmly ask what happened, so Devika learns she can own up without hiding 🙂

qa.q: Why might Devika have hidden under the dining table?
qa.a: She was probably frightened by the shouting and by what she had done, so hiding felt safer than explaining.

grounding: Shows a child working out that a younger sibling who broke a toy was scared rather than mean, while the anger only partly fades.
